en: To calm or pacify someone, often by giving in to their demands
bn: তুষ্ট করা; দাবি মেনে শান্ত করা
hook: APPEASE: give them 'A PEACE' offering so they stop fighting.
story: Appease. In the supermarket, four-year-old Babu threw himself on the floor and screamed for chocolate. Shoppers stared. His mother, red-faced, grabbed a chocolate bar from the shelf and handed it to him. The screaming stopped instantly. Babu smiled. Lesson learned: screaming works. To appease is to calm someone by giving in to their demands. In history, leaders who appeased aggressive dictators often encouraged even more aggression. Think: give them a peace offering.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the striking workers, management offered a modest raise, though it refused their central demand for shorter hours.
gre.clue: management offered a modest raise

en: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason
hook: ARBITRARY: like an ARBITER who decides by flipping a coin.
story: Arbitrary. The new hostel warden announced his rules. No showers after nine on Tuesdays. No blue shirts on Fridays. Guests allowed only on days ending in Y, except Wednesday. When students asked why, he said, "Because I said so." The rules were arbitrary: based on whim or chance rather than reason. An arbitrary decision feels unfair because nothing justifies it. Imagine a referee who decides every call by flipping a coin.

gre.s: Employees resented the new promotion policy, which seemed entirely ____, rewarding some workers and passing over others for no discernible reason.
gre.clue: for no discernible reason

en: Very old or old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use
hook: ARCHAIC: as old as ARCHAEOLOGY digs.
story: Archaic. Nadia's grandmother still writes letters the way she learned in 1962: "Henceforth, I beseech thee to partake of thy meals in a timely fashion." Her grandchildren giggle and read them aloud in dramatic voices. To modern ears the language sounds archaic: very old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier period and no longer in everyday use. Some laws are archaic too, written for a world that no longer exists. Think: as old as an archaeology dig.

gre.s: Although the statute remains on the books, it is so ____ that no court has enforced it in over a century.
gre.clue: no court has enforced it in over a century

en: Loud and noisy, often with insistent demands
hook: CLAMOROUS: CLAMOR, the loud cry of a crowd.
story: Clamorous. When the national cricket team landed with the trophy, the airport exploded. Drums thundered. Horns blared. Ten thousand fans chanted the captain's name and waved flags from every balcony, demanding that the players come out and wave. The police could barely hold the barricades. The crowd was clamorous: loudly noisy, often making insistent demands. Clamorous protesters demand action; clamorous children demand ice cream. A clamour is a loud, insistent outcry.

gre.s: The quiet library reading room offered a welcome refuge from the ____ market square outside, where vendors shouted their prices all day.
gre.clue: where vendors shouted their prices all day

en: A shortage or lack of something
hook: DEARTH: DEAR because there's so little of it, like EARTH in a desert.
story: Dearth. In a remote char village on the Jamuna, there is one clinic for twenty thousand people, open only twice a week. When children fall sick on other days, parents must travel three hours by boat to reach a doctor. The villagers do not complain about bad doctors. They complain that there are none. That is a dearth: a serious shortage or lack of something. GRE passages love phrases like "a dearth of evidence."

gre.s: Given the ____ of reliable records from the period, historians must rely heavily on a handful of surviving letters.
gre.clue: must rely heavily on a handful of surviving letters

en: Able to be explained or understood
hook: EXPLICABLE: can be EXPLAINED.
story: Explicable. Rafi's practice scores suddenly dropped from 315 to 298. His friends were puzzled. Was it bad luck? Was the test harder? Then his roommate mentioned that Rafi had been studying until four every morning and sleeping three hours a night. Suddenly the mystery was entirely explicable: able to be explained. Explicable is the opposite of the more familiar word inexplicable, meaning impossible to explain. Once you see the cause, a mystery becomes explicable.

gre.s: What at first seemed a baffling drop in sales became perfectly ____ once analysts noticed that a rival had launched a cheaper product that month.
gre.clue: once analysts noticed

en: Deliberate exaggeration for effect
hook: HYPER-BOLE: HYPER means over, too much. Over-the-top language.
story: Hyperbole. "I have told you a million times to clean your room!" Mitu's mother shouted. Mitu calmly replied, "Ammu, that is not true. You have said it maybe two hundred times." Her mother was not amused. She had not meant a million literally. She was using hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for effect. Hyper means over, too much. Advertisements are full of hyperbole: "the best tea in the universe!" Poets use it too.

gre.s: Although the critic called the film the worst ever made, her colleagues recognized the remark as ____ rather than a sober assessment.
gre.clue: rather than a sober assessment

en: Unchangeable over time
hook: IM-MUTABLE: can't MUTATE, can't change.
story: Immutable. Some things in life seem unchangeable. The sun rises in the east. Rivers flow toward the sea. Dhaka traffic is terrible. For centuries, scientists believed species were immutable too, fixed forever exactly as they were created. Then Darwin showed that they slowly change over time. Immutable means unchangeable. Im means not, mutable means able to change, as in mutation. Something immutable cannot mutate.

gre.s: Once regarded as ____ laws of nature, many of Newton's principles were later shown to require modification at very high speeds.
gre.clue: were later shown to require modification

en: Never tiring; persistently energetic
hook: IN-DE-FATIGABLE: cannot be FATIGUED.
story: Indefatigable. During the floods in Sylhet, a young relief worker named Tania worked eighteen hours a day for three weeks. She carried rice sacks on her back, rowed boats through flooded villages, comforted crying mothers, and still smiled at the volunteers every night. Nobody ever saw her tired. She was indefatigable: tireless, incapable of being worn out. In means not, fatigable means able to be fatigued. Fatigue never catches an indefatigable person.

gre.s: Even in her nineties, the ____ activist continued to march at every protest, outlasting colleagues half her age.
gre.clue: outlasting colleagues half her age

en: Lazy; avoiding activity or work
hook: INDOLENT: IN DOLE, living lazily on handouts without work.
story: Indolent. Tanvir's roommate slept until noon, ordered food instead of cooking, and left dishes piling up in the sink for a week. The fan blew dust across his unopened textbooks. When Tanvir asked him to help clean, he groaned, rolled over, and said, "Tomorrow." Tomorrow never came. He was indolent: habitually lazy, avoiding any effort. Indolent is a fancier synonym of slothful and idle, and a favourite GRE word.

gre.s: The governor was criticized as ____, preferring long holidays to the tedious work of governing while problems mounted at home.
gre.clue: preferring long holidays to the tedious work of governing

en: Narrow-minded and uninterested in outside ideas or cultures
hook: INSULAR: like an ISLAND (insula in Latin), cut off from the world.
story: Insular. In one remote village, people distrusted anyone from the next district. New foods were called dangerous. New music was called immoral. Visitors were watched with suspicion until they left. Nothing from outside was welcome. The community was insular: narrow-minded and uninterested in outside ideas or cultures, like an island cut off from the world. Insula means island in Latin. Insular communities often resist change.

gre.s: Critics accused the academic department of being ____, citing its refusal to engage with scholars from other disciplines or countries.
gre.clue: its refusal to engage with scholars from other disciplines or countries

en: Refusing to change one's views or to compromise
hook: IN-TRANSIGENT: won't TRANSit, won't move an inch.
story: Intransigent. The garment workers demanded a raise. The factory owner refused. The workers stopped work. The owner locked the gates. For three weeks, neither side moved a single inch, even as orders were cancelled and families went hungry. Every mediator who tried left frustrated. Both sides were intransigent: refusing to change their views or compromise. In means not, transigent relates to coming to terms. An intransigent negotiator kills every deal.

gre.s: Negotiations collapsed because both delegations remained ____, each refusing to modify even the most minor of its demands.
gre.clue: each refusing to modify even the most minor of its demands

en: Fearless and adventurous
hook: IN-TREPID: NOT trembling (trepidation = fear).
story: Intrepid. Wasfia Nazreen, a Bangladeshi mountaineer, climbed the highest peak on every continent. Storms tore at her tent. Frostbite threatened her fingers. The air near the summits was so thin that each step felt like a mile. She kept climbing. She was intrepid: fearless and adventurous. In means not, trepid relates to trepidation, meaning fear. An intrepid explorer goes where others are too afraid to go. Its opposite is timorous.

gre.s: The ____ journalist ventured into the war zone that other reporters had fled, sending back dispatches from the front lines.
gre.clue: that other reporters had fled

en: Showing a lack of respect for things usually taken seriously
hook: IR-REVERENT: not REVERENT, not respectful.
story: Irreverent. The comedian walked onto the stage and immediately made fun of the prime minister, the chief guest, a famous film star, and his own grandmother. Half the audience laughed until they cried. The other half gasped and clutched their pearls. His humour was irreverent: showing a lack of respect for things usually treated seriously or as sacred. Irreverent humour pokes fun at everything and everyone. Its opposite is reverent, meaning deeply respectful.

gre.s: The magazine was known for its ____ tone, mocking politicians, celebrities, and even its own editors with equal glee.
gre.clue: mocking politicians, celebrities, and even its own editors

en: To feel intense dislike or disgust for
hook: LOATHE: 'LOW-THE' — so low in your opinion that you hate it.
story: Loathe. Lamia loathes bitter gourd. One bite and her whole face twists as if she has swallowed poison. She would rather skip dinner entirely than eat it, and once hid a whole plate of it inside a flowerpot. To loathe is to hate something intensely, with disgust. Careful: loathe, ending in e, is the verb, to hate. Loath, without the e, is an adjective meaning reluctant. She was loath to eat it because she loathes it.

gre.s: Though he came to ____ the city's noise and crowds, the poet found he could not write anywhere else.
gre.clue: Though he came to

en: To speak harmful untruths about someone (verb); evil or harmful (adjective)
hook: MAL = bad. To say bad things about someone.
story: Malign. Jealous of her success, a rival shop owner began spreading rumours about Rahima. He told customers that she sold expired medicine and cheated on her taxes. None of it was true. Slowly, people stopped visiting her pharmacy. He had maligned her: spoken harmful untruths to damage her reputation. As an adjective, malign means evil or harmful, the opposite of benign. Mal means bad, as in malfunction and malice.

gre.s: Although tabloids continue to ____ the senator as corrupt, every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper.
gre.clue: every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper

en: Easily shaped or influenced; adaptable
hook: MALLEABLE: can be shaped with a MALLET (hammer).
story: Malleable. In the goldsmith's workshop in Tanti Bazar, Joya watched in amazement as the old craftsman hammered a single gram of gold into a sheet so thin that light shone through it. It never cracked. Gold is malleable: easily shaped without breaking. Children's minds are malleable too, shaped easily by what they see and hear. A malleable person can be easily persuaded. Think: it can be shaped with a mallet, a hammer.

gre.s: Adolescents' opinions are often more ____ than those of adults, shifting readily in response to friends and media.
gre.clue: shifting readily in response to friends and media

en: A beginner; a person new to a subject or activity
hook: NEO = new, PHYTE = plant. A newly planted sprout.
story: Neophyte. On his first morning at the gym, Imran did not know how to adjust a single machine. He lifted with his back instead of his legs, put the treadmill on the highest incline by mistake, and nearly dropped a dumbbell on his foot. The trainer laughed kindly. "Everyone starts as a neophyte." A neophyte is a beginner, someone new to a skill or subject. Neo means new, phyte means plant: a freshly planted sprout.

gre.s: Though only a ____ at chess, having learned the rules a month earlier, the girl stunned the club by defeating its champion.
gre.clue: having learned the rules a month earlier

en: Easily shaped or molded; flexible and adaptable
hook: GRE trick: PLASTIC means moldable, like clay — not just the material.
story: Plastic. Neuroscientists say a child's brain is plastic: it rewires itself constantly, learns languages easily, and can even recover after an injury by sending signals along new paths. On the GRE, plastic rarely means a shopping bag. It means moldable, flexible, and able to be shaped. Clay is plastic; stone is not. Plastic surgery originally meant surgery that reshapes the body. Plastic arts, like sculpture, shape material with the hands.

gre.s: Contrary to the old belief that the adult brain is fixed, researchers now regard it as remarkably ____, capable of forming new connections throughout life.
gre.clue: capable of forming new connections throughout life

en: A remark used too often to be interesting or meaningful
hook: PLATITUDE: a FLAT attitude remark; flat, dull, overused.
story: Platitude. When Kamal failed his driving test, everyone had something to say. "Everything happens for a reason." "Failure is the key to success." "Just stay positive." "Tomorrow is another day." Each sentence was meant to comfort him. None of them helped at all. They were platitudes: remarks used so often that they have become dull and meaningless. Think: a flat attitude. Political speeches are often full of platitudes.

gre.s: The commencement speaker disappointed the graduates by offering nothing but ____, urging them to follow their dreams and never give up.
gre.clue: urging them to follow their dreams and never give up

en: Having knowledge of events before they happen
bn: দূরদর্শী; ভবিষ্যৎ আগে থেকে জানে এমন
hook: PRE-SCIENT: knowing (scient, science) beforehand.
story: Prescient. In 2015, Arif's uncle told the whole family to learn digital skills. "One day," he said, "offices will close, and everyone will work from home on the internet." They laughed at him. Five years later, a pandemic shut every office, and the cousins who had learned coding kept their jobs. His advice had been prescient: showing knowledge of events before they happen. Pre means before, scient means knowing, as in science.

gre.s: The novel now seems remarkably ____, having described smartphones and social media decades before either existed.
gre.clue: decades before either existed

en: In its original, perfect condition; completely clean
hook: PRISTINE: PRIS-TEEN, as fresh and new as a teen.
story: Pristine. When Sara first visited Saint Martin's Island as a child, the beaches were pristine: white sand, clear turquoise water, coral glowing beneath the waves, and not a single plastic bottle in sight. Last year she returned. Wrappers drifted in the shallows and hotels crowded the shore. Pristine means in perfect, original condition, untouched and completely clean. A pristine copy of an old book has no marks at all.

gre.s: Conservationists are fighting to protect one of the last ____ forests on the continent, a wilderness never touched by logging or roads.
gre.clue: never touched by logging or roads

en: To express disapproval or disappointment to someone
hook: REPROACH: re-APPROACH someone to tell them they disappointed you.
story: Reproach. Tanvir forgot his mother's birthday. Completely. That evening, she did not shout. She simply looked at him with sad, quiet eyes and said, "I waited all evening for your call." Then she went back to cooking. That single look hurt more than any scolding. To reproach is to express disappointment or disapproval to someone. A look of reproach can be devastating. Beyond reproach means so perfect that nobody can criticize you.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the young employee for his mistake, the manager calmly showed him how to avoid it in the future.
gre.clue: calmly showed him how to avoid it in the future

en: Strong, sturdy, and healthy; vigorous
hook: ROBUST: like a ROBOT, strong and hard to break.
story: Robust. Farhan's father still uses an old Nokia phone from 2006. It has fallen off the roof, been run over by a bicycle, and spent a whole night in a monsoon puddle. Every time, it switched on and rang. The family calls it the brick. It is robust: strong, sturdy, and hard to break. Robust health, a robust economy, robust evidence: all of them can withstand pressure. Think of a robot built to last.

gre.s: Far from being fragile, the economy proved surprisingly ____, recovering within months from a shock that analysts had expected to last years.
gre.clue: Far from being fragile

en: Promoting health; wholesome
hook: SALUBRIOUS: SALUTE to health, as in 'salud!'
story: Salubrious. Doctors told Rafi's grandfather that Dhaka's smoky air was ruining his lungs. So the family moved him to a small house in the hills of Sylhet: fresh breezes, clean spring water, quiet nights, and morning walks through the tea gardens. Within months he was breathing easily and walking two kilometres a day. The climate was salubrious: good for health. Think of the toast salud, meaning health. Salubrious food and salubrious habits keep you well.

gre.s: Wealthy Victorians flocked to the seaside resort, convinced that its ____ air could cure everything from asthma to melancholy.
gre.clue: could cure everything from asthma to melancholy

en: To give official approval to; also, a penalty for breaking a rule
hook: SANCTION has two opposite meanings: APPROVAL and PUNISHMENT. Watch the context!
story: Sanction. On Monday, the university sanctioned the new robotics club: it officially approved the club, gave it a room, and assigned it a budget. On Tuesday, the United Nations imposed sanctions on a country that had violated a treaty: penalties restricting its trade. Same word, opposite meanings. Sanction can mean approval or punishment. The GRE loves this kind of word. Read the context carefully, and do not assume.

gre.s: Although the council refused to formally ____ the festival, it took no action to stop the residents from holding it.
gre.clue: it took no action to stop the residents

en: Showing dedication and diligence; persistent
hook: SEDULOUS: SEATED-ulous, seated at the desk all day, diligently working.
story: Sedulous. Every morning at six, before her family woke, Nadia sat at her desk with tea and flashcards. Every evening after work, she completed a quant set. Every Saturday, a full practice test. Six months, no skipped days, not even on Eid morning. When she earned a perfect verbal score, nobody was surprised. She had been sedulous: diligent, dedicated, and persevering. Picture someone seated at the desk all day. Sedulous is a synonym of assiduous.

gre.s: Only through ____ effort, poring over thousands of documents for more than a decade, did the historian reconstruct the lost trade route.
gre.clue: poring over thousands of documents for more than a decade

en: Tending to make you sleepy
hook: SOPORIFIC: SO POOR, a lecture so poor it makes you sleepy.
story: Soporific. Professor Karim taught economics in a slow, flat voice for two straight hours, reading every word directly from his slides. The ceiling fan hummed. The room was warm. Within twenty minutes, half the class was asleep, heads drooping onto notebooks. One student actually snored. His lectures were soporific: tending to make people sleepy. Warm milk is soporific; so are some medicines. Think: so poor a lecture that it puts you to sleep.

gre.s: Even the most enthusiastic students found the lecturer's monotone delivery ____, and many dozed off before the first hour had ended.
gre.clue: many dozed off

en: Serious, strict, and unyielding
hook: STERN: like the STERN (back) of a ship, firm and unmoving.
story: Stern. When the principal walked into the assembly hall, eight hundred students stopped talking instantly. She did not smile. She did not raise her voice. She simply stood at the front, hands folded, and looked at the latecomers. Every one of them felt that look. Her face was stern: serious, strict, and unyielding. A stern warning means you had better listen. Think of the stern of a ship: firm, solid, and not moving.

gre.s: Behind the judge's ____ exterior, which intimidated many lawyers, lay a deeply compassionate person.
gre.clue: which intimidated many lawyers

en: Promoting a particular point of view, especially a controversial one; biased
hook: TENDENTIOUS: has a TENDENCY to favor one side.
story: Tendentious. The documentary claimed to be neutral. But it interviewed only one side, played dramatic, sinister music whenever the other side appeared, and quietly left out facts that did not fit its argument. Viewers noticed. Critics called it tendentious: written or presented to promote a particular, often controversial, point of view; biased. Think: it has a tendency to lean one way. GRE passages sometimes describe a tendentious reading of history.

gre.s: The reviewer dismissed the study as ____, noting that its authors had selected only the evidence that supported their political agenda.
gre.clue: selected only the evidence that supported their political agenda
